newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Food prices soar in Afghan capital Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Food prices soar in Afghan capital Kabul.

text.p: The price of wheatflour has risen by more than 60 percent over the past two weeks in the Afghan capital Kabul as supplies from Pakistan have dried up, traders said on Monday.

"A 100 kilogramme (225 lb) bag of flour was 550,000 Afghanis ($25.50), but for the last three or four days it has been 900,000 Afghanis ($41.00)," said Naderi, a flour trader in Kabul's Karte Parwan market.

"Pakistan has closed all the borders for export of wheat flour to Afghanistan. Almost 80 per cent of Afghanistan's flour comes from Pakistan," he said. "The price might go up again tomorrow if we don't get more supplies." Pakistan has clamped down on the export of wheat flour to Afghanistan because of severe shortages in their domestic market.
Terry Pitzner of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees told Reuters the food situation in Kabul had already become critical before the price rises.
"Bread is the staple food for most families. We were already seriously concerned about the situation in the city before," said Pitzner.

"We have over 140,000 displaced people in the city from the plains to the north, we have had to spread our already stretched resources to include these people. We are looking at a steadily deteriorating situation."
"In the last two weeks we have had more aid trucks carrying wheat into Afghanistan than commercial trucks," he added.
The U.N. estimates that almost half of Kabul's one million population already receives some kind of food aid from the international community.
Pitzner said the number of people needing aid was steadily climbing.
"The middle class have become poor and the poor have become destitute," he said.
In the wake of the price rises, Kabul's bakeries have maintained the price of their long, flat loaves of unleavened bread at 1,000 Afghanis (5 cents), but have cut the weight.
"We have cut the weight of our loaves from 180 grammes (6.5 ounces) to 135 grammes (4.5 ounces) since the price of wheat flour went up," said baker Zulmai.
After almost five years of civil war that has battered the capital, Kabul's economy has collapsed, and many people are forced to survive on bread alone.
Aziz Malek, a mason, came to the bakery to buy his lunch.
"Look at the size of this," he said, holding up the single loaf that was all he could afford to purchase.

"It wouldn't feed a child. I have got ten people in my family to feed, and on a monthly salary of 150,000 Afghanis ($6.80) there is not much I can afford except bread, and sometimes a little tea," said Malek.
